title: Detection of Web Services
summary: This detection strategy looks for the registration and use of attacker-controlled web services, the stage where an adversary buys a domain, stands up hosting, and points a web service at it before any payload is delivered. It covers technique T1583.006, which matters because this infrastructure is often the only durable thread linking separate intrusions: payloads change, but the domain and its certificate often persist. The telemetry that makes it possible is passive Domain Name System (DNS) resolution data, certificate transparency logs, WHOIS and registrar records, and outbound web proxy or firewall logs. In practice the strategy fails for two reasons: legitimate marketing teams register dozens of new domains each week, and modern hosting sits behind shared content delivery networks, so a single IP address reputation signal is weak. Analysts therefore score several weak signals together, such as domain age, certificate age, hosting provider, and the shape of the domain name itself.

beginner.definition: A web service is a site on the internet that an attacker controls. This detection looks for new domains and new hosting that appear before an attack. It tries to spot the attacker's site early, before anyone visits it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers need somewhere to put their fake login pages and stolen files. That place is usually a domain they just bought. If you can find the domain early, you can block the whole campaign at once. A blocked domain protects every user, even users you have not checked yet. This is why the earliest signal is often the most valuable one.
howItWorks: You collect Domain Name System (DNS) records. These records show which name points to which internet address.
You collect certificate transparency logs. A certificate is a digital identity paper for a website.
You check how old each domain is. A domain registered three days ago is more interesting than one registered in 2011.
You score the name itself. Long random names, many numbers and odd endings all raise the score.
You compare the hosting address with known bad infrastructure or with an unusual provider.
You send the highest scores to an analyst to review by hand.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman who walks the street before the shops open. He is not looking for a thief inside a shop yet. He is looking for a new shop sign that went up overnight, with no stock inside and no customers. A domain that was registered yesterday does the same thing. It is a new sign on the street, and it often means someone is getting ready to do something.
takeaways: This detection finds attacker infrastructure before the attack starts.
One weak signal is not enough. You combine domain age, name shape and hosting.
Blocking an early domain can stop a whole campaign at once.

objectives: Explain how domain registration and certificate data can reveal attacker infrastructure before a payload is delivered
Identify the fields in DNS and certificate transparency records that indicate a newly created web service
Describe why content delivery networks and shared hosting weaken address based reputation checks
Build a scored alert that combines domain age, name entropy and hosting reputation instead of a single indicator
Plan a baseline of legitimate domain registrations so that marketing and product launches do not drown the queue
Decide when a newly observed domain justifies a block at the web proxy rather than passive monitoring
dataSources: Passive DNS resolution records linking queried domain names to resolved IP addresses with first seen and last seen timestamps
Certificate transparency log entries containing newly issued certificates, subject common names and issuing certificate authority
WHOIS and registrar records with domain creation date, registrant country and name server delegation
Outbound web proxy or secure web gateway logs containing the requested fully qualified domain name, user agent and bytes transferred
Firewall or netflow records of outbound connections to external IP addresses with destination autonomous system number
logic: The pattern is a web service that is new and unknown at the moment it is first contacted from the estate. You correlate the fully qualified domain name observed in DNS query logs or web proxy logs with enrichment that carries domain creation age, certificate age, hosting autonomous system and a name randomness score. The malicious case is a domain seen for the first time in the estate within days of its registration, resolving to hosting that the organisation has never used, often with a name that carries no brand or dictionary meaning. The benign case is a domain that is either old, delegated to a well known software as a service provider, or part of a product launch that has been announced in change records. No single field decides the alert; the score only becomes actionable when recent registration, unfamiliar hosting and first contact from the estate appear together.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Newly Registered Domain Contacted From the Estate
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: dns
# detection:
#   selection:
#     query_type: A
#     domain_age_days: < 30
#     domain_entropy: > 3.5
#   filter:
#     domain|endswith:
#       - .microsoft.com
#       - .amazonaws.com
#       - .corp.example
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Marketing or brand campaigns that register a short lived landing page domain days before a public launch
Cloud development sandboxes that create a new randomised subdomain for every ephemeral test environment
Third party SaaS trials where the trial tenant is provisioned on a brand new domain not yet seen in the estate
Regional subsidiary domains registered by the legal team for a new trading entity
Content delivery networks that serve customer specific hostnames on freshly issued certificates
tuningNotes: Start by building a thirty day baseline of every newly registered domain that the estate actually contacts, grouped by business unit and hosting provider, then allowlist the providers and campaign domains that appear as legitimate. Scope the rule to user workstation and browser traffic rather than server subnets, because servers legitimately reach many new partner endpoints. Add a filter for domains whose certificate was issued to the same organisation as the requesting host. Narrowing this way trades away visibility of attacker infrastructure that reuses a legitimate hosting provider, so keep a lower severity version of the rule that alerts on first contact alone for high value users such as executives and administrators.
